Stage 3 · Grammar

Second conditional

Talking about something that is not true, and saying what would follow.

Read these four sentences from the recording.
  • If scientists were more intelligent, they would find more cures.
  • The world would be a better place if everybody learned to dance.
  • I would take a smart pill if I knew it was safe.
  • If only a few people could afford them, that would give them an unfair advantage.
The verb after if is in the past form. Is the speaker talking about the past?
The pattern
 The if part — not trueThe result part — what would follow
Order 1If I had more time,I would learn to dance.
Order 2I would learn to dance if I had more time.  —  same meaning, no comma
NegativeIf she didn’t work at weekends,she wouldn’t be so tired.
QuestionWhat would you do if you won the money?  ·  Would you move if they offered you the job?
Short answerYes, I would. / No, I wouldn’t.
beIf I were you, I’d say no.  —  were for every person; was is also heard, but write were.
Softer resultthat could give them an advantage · it might not work  —  could and might replace would when you are less sure
if + past form would + verb

FORM. if + Past Simple, would + plain verb. Either half can come first.

USE. The situation is not true now, or is very unlikely. The past form is the signal for “imagine”, not for past time.

BE. If I were you… — were for every person.

Not “If I would have money”, not “If I will be rich”, not “If I had money, I will buy…”

Compare with the first conditional from Unit 9: If it rains, I’ll stay in — that one is possible. This one is not.

FORM. if + Past Simple  +  would + the plain verb. If I had more time, I would learn to dance. You can turn it round — I would learn to dance if I had more time — and the meaning does not change. When the if half comes first, put a comma after it; when it comes second, no comma.

USE. This is the “imagine” tense. The past form does not mean past time here — it is the grammar’s way of saying this is not the case. If I had more time means I do not have more time. If I were you means I am not you. English marks the unreal by stepping the verb back one tense.

COMPARE. If it rains tomorrow, I’ll stay in. — rain is quite possible, so first conditional. If it snowed in July, I’d be amazed. — that is not going to happen, so second conditional. The choice is not about time. It is about how likely you think it is.

WERE, NOT WAS. With be, careful English uses were for every person: If he were here…, If I were you…. You will hear was in speech and nobody will mind, but write were.

SOFTER RESULTS. Swap would for could or might when you are less certain: If we planted more trees, it might help.

The three mistakes to watch: “If I would have money” (never would in the if half) · “If I will be rich” (no future in the if half either) · “If I had money, I will buy a house” (mixing the two conditionals).

The judge’s own words, from the coursebook recording.

Full grammar reference — The second conditional

Form

StructureIf + Past Simple, would + plain verb
ExampleIf I had more time, I would learn Arabic.
were for everybodyIf I were you, I’d take the job.
NegativeIf she didn’t work nights, she wouldn’t be so tired.
QuestionWhat would you do if you won the money?

Spelling and sound

would → ’d · would not → wouldn’t. The Past Simple after if is not about the past.

When and why we use it

  • The second conditional talks about a situation that is imaginary, unlikely or impossible now.
  • The past form after if is a signal of distance from reality, not a signal of past time.
  • Could and might can replace would: If I had the money, I could travel.
  • If I were you is the standard way of giving advice.

Signal words

if · would · imagine · suppose · in an ideal world

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • If I would have money, I would travel. → If I had money, I would travel.Would only in the result clause.
  • If I was you, I’d wait. → If I were you, I’d wait.Fixed phrase.
  • If she came, I would been happy. → … I would be happy.Plain verb after would.
  • What you would do? → What would you do?Auxiliary before the subject.

Don’t confuse it with

First conditional = real: If it rains, I’ll stay in. Second = imaginary: If it snowed in July, I’d be amazed.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

The year the United Nations asked the world what to fix first.

Before you read: the UN asked people in almost every country to choose the six things that would make the most difference to their lives. What do you think came first?

A prediction, not an answer. The text tells you in paragraph two.

One question, seven million answers

Before the United Nations agreed its development goals for 2030, it did something unusual: it asked the world what to put in them. The survey was called MY World. It gave people a list of sixteen issues, from a good education to action on climate change, and asked one question: if you could choose only six, which six would make the most difference to your life? By the end of 2014 more than seven million people, on every continent, had voted; most of them voted on paper. It is still one of the largest surveys ever carried out.

The answer was not the one many people in Europe expected. First came a good education. Then better healthcare, and then better job opportunities. An honest and responsive government was high on the list in every region. Affordable food — the hunger question — sat in the middle. Political freedoms, reliable energy at home, and phone and internet access came near the bottom — and so did action on climate change.

That last result needs care. It does not mean that the world thinks global warming is not an issue. When the researchers looked at rich and poor countries separately, they found a clear financial pattern: the richer the country, the higher climate action was placed. If you had secure work, clean water and a school for your children, you would have room to think about the coral reef and the natural disaster. If you did not, you would choose the school.

A list like this is powerful because nobody chose it for the voters. If the survey ran again today, the order might change, but the top probably would not. And if you could change one thing about the world, what would it be?

Sources. UN MY World survey, run by UNDP, the UN Millennium Campaign, the Overseas Development Institute and the World Wide Web Foundation; results published 2013–2015. From those published results: the list of sixteen issues and the choice of six; the top three priorities; the position of climate action, political freedoms and internet access at the bottom; the vote total by the end of 2014; and the finding that the priority given to climate action rises with a country’s level of development. Written for this course; no wording is taken from the reports.

Stage 7 · Now you

Your sixty seconds

Same programme, same rules. One idea, one minute, then it gets scored.

Useful language

The idea — My idea to change the world is… · I would like to change the world by… · The world would be a better place if…

The reason — Why would this be a good idea? · First of all… · Another thing is that… · If we did this, … would…

Judging it — I like the idea that… · My worry, though, is… · True, but if you…, then you… · I’d give it … out of 10.

1 · Take two minutes and prepare your own sixty-second idea.

Use at least two second conditionals. Write notes only — you will speak, not read.

Say what the idea is, then why it would work, then what would change if everybody did it.

2 · Work in groups of three. Two present, one judges. Then rotate.
Card A — presenter

You have 60 seconds and somebody is timing you. Say your idea in the first sentence — do not build up to it. Give two reasons. Finish with what the world would look like if it happened.

Card B — judge

Listen without interrupting. Then say one thing you liked, one worry, and a score out of 10. Use My worry, though, is… and True, but if you… Do not just say “good idea”.

Rotate until everyone has presented once and judged once. The judging is where the grammar comes back.
